Medical Neuroanatomy · Chapter 4 · Case Study 4-1

Occipital Headache, Vertigo, and a Slowly Declaring Brainstem Syndrome

A 59-year-old man with three days of fluctuating dizziness, diplopia, and right-hand clumsiness
Annotated case notes · tap or click any highlight to open the explanation
Localization Finding Term Pattern Trajectory
hover (desktop) for a quick preview · tap/click for the full explanation

Chief Complaint

A 59-year-old, right-handed male was admitted to the hospital with a chief complaint of occipital headaches and several periods of dizziness and loss of balance over the past 2 days.

History of Chief Complaint

Three days prior to admission, the patient noted a sudden onset of diplopia on forward gaze and a sensation of dizziness. These complaints resolved within twenty-four hours. He experienced several episodes of dizziness and diplopia over the next 24 hours. One day prior to admission he noted a relatively sudden onset of dizziness, diplopia and clumsiness in the right hand. These complaints have persisted since that time although he states that the dizziness seems to be improving slightly.

Medical History

The patient had been under treatment for hypertension for 6 years duration, with observed blood pressures in the range of 180/110.

General Physical Examination

The patient was alert, oriented, and cooperative; he was a well-nourished man of medium height who appeared his stated age. Funduscopic examination revealed clear optic discs with sharp borders. The external auditory canal was patent and uninflamed. Pharynx and larynx were non-reddened. A grade II/VI bruit was present over the right carotid artery. His blood pressure was elevated (192/96). Peripheral pulses were intact at the ankle and wrist. Respirations were normal. His chest was clear to auscultation; skin was warm and of normal texture; abdomen was soft with no tenderness, lumps, or masses. Extremities were four in number with no edema present; no lymphadenopathy was present in the cervical or inguinal areas.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status

The patient was awake and oriented with respect to person, place, and time. Memory was appropriate for his age. Speech was hoarse, but articulate and meaningful. He could follow three- and four-step commands.

Cranial Nerves

Extraocular movements were full, but he complained of diplopia made worse by lateral gaze to the left. Nystagmus was present on left lateral gaze. The right pupil measured 3 mm, the left was 5 mm, but both responded to light and accommodation. Ptosis of the right eyelid and decreased sweating on the right side of the face (anhidrosis) were also present. Hearing was diminished in both ears to high frequencies. He admitted to a feeling of dizziness that he described as the world moving around him. Pain, but not touch sensation, was decreased on the right side of the face with the exception of some sparing around the lips and nasal region. The right corneal reflex was diminished. He complained of a paroxysmal tingling sensation on the left side of his face that he described as occasionally being painful. Facial expressions were full and symmetric. The uvula deviated to the left, and there was deficient elevation of the right side of the palate. There was also a suggestion of hoarseness in his speech.

Motor System

Strength was intact throughout his body; deep tendon reflexes were intact and symmetric in all extremities. A mild ataxia was evident in the right upper extremity on finger-tapping, hand-patting, and finger-to-nose tests. An intention tremor was present. A slight ataxia was also detectable in the right lower extremity on heel-to-shin and tibia-tapping tests. These movements in the upper and lower extremity became noticeably worse when he closed his eyes.

Sensory Exam

He had a mild analgesia to pinprick on the left side of the body, the left arm, and the left leg. Position, vibration, and touch modalities were intact throughout the entire body.

Follow-Up

Examination of the patient two months after this event found most of his complaints have resolved with the exception of a mild right-sided facial analgesia, greatest along the angle of his jaw. Although he no longer complained of clumsiness, finger-to-nose testing demonstrated a mild persistent dysmetria.

Questions

  1. Has the patient experienced any changes in consciousness or cognition, language function or spatial recognition, personality or emotional behavior, or any loss in memory?
  2. Does the patient exhibit any loss of vision, and if so, where in the visual field is the loss? Are there any visual hallucinations present in this patient?
  3. Are there any changes in cranial nerve function and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  4. Are there any changes in motor function such as reflexes, muscle tone, movement, or coordination and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  5. Are there any changes in sensory function and if so, what levels of the body have experienced this change?
  6. What is the clinical temporal profile of this patient's neurologic problem: is the onset of neurologic findings acute or insidious, is the course of the neurologic disease chronically progressive, fluctuant or stable?
  7. Based on the presenting signs and symptoms do you think the distribution of the neurologic pathology is focal, multifocal or diffuse?
  8. Based on the answers to these questions develop a differential diagnosis of the patient's neurological problem?
  9. If the origin of the pathology is vascular, what arterial supply is most likely involved with the lesion in this patient?
ReasoningClinical Reasoning Walkthrough

Localization

Every positive finding in this exam clusters in one place: the right dorsolateral medulla. The crossed pattern of ipsilateral face / contralateral body sensory loss, the ipsilateral Horner's triad, the ipsilateral bulbar signs (hoarseness, palatal droop), and the ipsilateral limb ataxia all point to structures that run together in the lateral medullary tegmentum — the vestibular nuclei, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, nucleus ambiguus, descending sympathetic fibers, the restiform body (inferior cerebellar peduncle) with its spinocerebellar afferents, and the anterolateral system as it ascends through this level. Two negatives complete the picture: fully preserved strength/reflexes (Question 4) rule out the corticospinal tract in the ventral medulla, and fully preserved position/vibration/touch (Question 5) rule out the medially-placed dorsal column–medial lemniscus system. This is a segmental (brainstem) lesion, not a suprasegmental one (Question 3) — mental status, language, and personality are entirely untouched (Question 1), and there is no visual field loss or hallucination reported (Question 2), so the occipital headache is a vascular-territory clue, not evidence of an occipital lobe lesion.

Distribution

Focal (Question 7). A single, unilateral lesion confined to the right dorsolateral medulla accounts for the entire exam — there is no evidence of multifocal disease (no findings outside this one territory) or a diffuse process (no encephalopathy, no bilateral or symmetric findings other than the incidental bilateral high-frequency hearing loss, which is age-related and non-localizing).

Time Course

Subacute and stepwise (Question 6) — not a single acute event and not chronically progressive. A self-limited episode three days before admission, several more episodes over the following day, then a final event one day before admission that left a persistent deficit: this crescendo-TIA-to-completed-infarct pattern is characteristic of large-vessel vertebrobasilar atherothrombotic disease, distinct from the single abrupt onset of embolic stroke or the slow, unremitting progression expected from a tumor.

Differential Diagnosis

DiagnosisFitsArgues against
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — PICA / vertebral artery territoryMost likely Explains every finding in one focal, right dorsolateral medullary territory; stepwise crescendo-TIA course; strong vascular risk factors (long-standing hypertension, elevated presenting BP, atherosclerosis suggested by the carotid bruit) None significant
Vestibular neuritis / labyrinthitis Vertigo, nystagmus Cannot explain crossed sensory loss, Horner's syndrome, palatal/vocal cord weakness, or limb ataxia
Medial medullary syndrome Also a brainstem vascular event Strength and reflexes are intact (medial medullary syndrome produces contralateral limb weakness); no tongue deviation from hypoglossal involvement
Multiple sclerosis (brainstem plaque) Can produce a combined brainstem syndrome Atypical age for a first presentation; stepwise-to-fixed course over days plus strong vascular risk factors favor stroke over a demyelinating event
Posterior fossa mass / tumor Can cause combined cranial nerve and cerebellar findings Onset over days is far too rapid for typical tumor growth; no signs of raised intracranial pressure; symptoms partially fluctuated and improved, which a mass lesion would not do
Primary cerebellar hemorrhage or infarct Vertigo, ataxia Does not account for the crossed body sensory loss, Horner's syndrome, or the lower cranial nerve (bulbar) findings

Diagnostic Workup

  1. Non-contrast CT head.First priority in any acute stroke presentation — excludes hemorrhage before anything else, including any consideration of antithrombotic therapy.
  2. MRI brain with DWI, posterior fossa protocol.CT is notoriously insensitive to brainstem infarcts; diffusion-weighted MRI confirms the infarct and its exact territory.
  3. MRA or CTA of the head and neck.Evaluates the vertebral arteries and PICA for stenosis, occlusion, or dissection — and separately characterizes the incidentally noted right carotid disease.
  4. Carotid duplex ultrasound.Further quantifies the grade II/VI carotid bruit, even though the anterior circulation isn't the source of this presentation.
  5. Echocardiogram (TTE, with TEE if indicated) and cardiac telemetry.Screens for a cardioembolic source (e.g., atrial fibrillation) that could overlap with or mimic large-vessel disease.
  6. Fasting lipid panel and HbA1c/glucose.Characterizes the modifiable metabolic contributors to his atherosclerotic risk.
  7. Bedside, then formal, swallow evaluation.Nucleus ambiguus involvement (hoarseness, palatal weakness) carries a real aspiration risk — assess before resuming oral intake.

Prognosis

Lateral medullary syndrome carries a relatively favorable prognosis among brainstem strokes, precisely because it spares the corticospinal tract — this patient never lost strength. Most acute deficits (vertigo, diplopia, most of the sensory loss) substantially improve over weeks to months through central compensation, exactly as seen at the two-month follow-up. The findings that do tend to linger — patchy facial sensory loss and limb dysmetria, both present here — reflect the slower, often incomplete recovery of the spinal trigeminal tract and cerebellar-pathway (restiform body) function relative to other structures in this syndrome.

Management

  • NPO until swallow evaluation clears him, given the aspiration risk from bulbar (nucleus ambiguus) involvement
  • Vestibular rehabilitation and PT/OT for gait training and limb ataxia
  • Antiplatelet therapy (e.g., aspirin) once hemorrhage is excluded on imaging
  • Permissive hypertension acutely, then treatment of his chronic hypertension once stable
  • High-intensity statin therapy for atherosclerotic risk reduction
  • Work-up and management of the carotid stenosis identified incidentally (surveillance vs. intervention, per duplex findings)
  • Long-term secondary-prevention risk factor modification (blood pressure, lipids, glucose)
Deep DiveConcept Deep-Dives
Localization

Mapping the Lesion: The Right Dorsolateral Medulla

Bottom line: one infarct, one arterial territory, nine findings. A single lesion in the right PICA / vertebral artery distribution explains the vertigo and nystagmus, the Horner's triad, the hoarseness and palatal droop, the ipsilateral limb ataxia, and the crossed face/body sensory split — while cleanly sparing strength and dorsal-column sensation. Recognizing that an entire exam can collapse into one small vascular territory is the central pattern-recognition move this case is built to teach.
Localization

Anterolateral System (Spinothalamic Tract)

Tied to this patient: his left-sided pinprick analgesia — with position, vibration, and touch completely intact — is exactly what a right-sided anterolateral system lesion predicts. These fibers have already crossed in the spinal cord before ascending, so a right medullary lesion produces contralateral pain/temperature loss, while the separate, more medially-located dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway carrying position and vibration sense is left untouched.
Localization

Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus & Tract

From the small group
Why "oral-nasal sparing" happens, worked through level by level: think of the nucleus as a column with the most rostral part (pars oralis) representing the region around the mouth and nose, and the most caudal part (pars caudalis, blending into the cervical dorsal horn) representing the outer face near the jaw and ear — the reverse of what you'd guess from body position. A caudal lesion only knocks out the caudal (jaw/ear) representation, because the oral-nasal fibers have already peeled off and synapsed higher up — that's oral-nasal sparing. A lesion catching the already-crossed, ascending second-order fibers (the ventral trigeminothalamic tract) produces a contralateral deficit instead — but because those crossed fibers are spread thin and diffuse at this level rather than bundled tightly, a partial hit there tends to produce paresthesia ("pins and needles"), not complete analgesia. Only once all the fibers — ipsilateral descending and already-crossed ascending — converge into one discrete, dense tract higher in the brain stem does a lesion produce a complete, contralateral loss.
Tied to this patient: his ipsilateral right facial analgesia with sparing around the lips and nose is the caudal-lesion pattern above — consistent with the lesion sitting relatively low in the spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus. And two months later, the one deficit that persisted was analgesia along the angle of the jaw — the most caudal, and per this same somatotopy, often the most durably affected part of the map.
Pattern

The Oculosympathetic Pathway & Horner's Syndrome

From the small group
Horner's ptosis vs. CN III palsy ptosis — don't confuse them: the eyelid has two openers. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) does the actual lifting and initiating of eye-opening; the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle — smooth muscle, sympathetically innervated — only holds the lid fully retracted once it's open. In Horner's syndrome only the sympathetic input is lost, so the patient can still initiate opening the eye; the ptosis is partial and the eye is not pointing "down and out." In a CN III palsy, the lid can't be lifted at all, and the eye deviates down-and-out from unopposed lateral rectus/superior oblique action — a fully different, complete ptosis. One more common misconception the small group flagged directly: Horner's syndrome does not cause dry eye — anhidrosis is a loss of sweating, not tearing, so lacrimation stays normal.
Tied to this patient: right ptosis + miosis (the smaller, 3 mm pupil) + anhidrosis is the complete Horner's triad. Because the lesion here is central — interrupting first-order fibers in the brain stem rather than the ganglion or its peripheral branches — it appears alongside the rest of the brainstem findings rather than as an isolated sign, which is exactly the pattern that should raise suspicion for a central (not peripheral) cause of Horner's syndrome.
Finding

Nucleus Ambiguus & the Lower Cranial Nerves (IX, X, XI)

Tied to this patient: his hoarseness and the palate that fails to elevate on the right (pulling the uvula to the left, away from the lesion) are the two bedside signs of a unilateral nucleus ambiguus lesion. Because this nucleus also drives swallowing, a lesion here carries real aspiration risk — which is exactly why a swallow evaluation belongs at the top of this patient's acute management, before any oral intake resumes.
Finding

Restiform Body & the Spinocerebellar Pathway → Ipsilateral Ataxia

Tied to this patient: spinocerebellar afferents entering through the restiform body never cross before reaching the cerebellum, so damage here produces ataxia ipsilateral to the lesion — precisely why his incoordination showed up in the right hand and right leg, the same side as everything else in this syndrome except the crossed pain/temperature loss. The worsening with eyes closed layers in a second, vestibular contribution from the adjacent vestibular nuclei, and it's this cerebellar-pathway component that also explains why his dysmetria was the one motor finding still present at two-month follow-up.
Pattern

Textbook Reference: Lateral Medullary Syndrome

From the small group
The small group's own mnemonic for the vascular territory: "Don't pick a PICA horse (hoarseness) that can't eat (dysphagia)." The pathology is vascular — typically thrombotic, with a prodrome of crescendo TIAs like this patient's — from occlusion of the PICA or vertebral artery. It's rarely the main trunk of either vessel that's occluded (that would cause a much larger, more devastating infarct); more often it's one of the small penetrating branches those vessels give off, which is why the deficit stays confined to one dorsolateral territory and why recovery, once collateral flow or clot resolution restores supply, can be as complete as it was here.
Why "alternating" analgesia is the cardinal sign: the dorsolateral medulla is the only level of the neuraxis where the ipsilateral (not-yet-crossed) facial pain pathway and the contralateral (already-crossed) body pain pathway run right next to each other. Damage above this level — once the trigeminal fibers have crossed into the ventral trigeminothalamic tract in the pons/midbrain — makes everything ipsilateral again; damage below it loses facial representation entirely and leaves only a body-only pattern. The crossed-face/crossed-body split is a one-level phenomenon, and this patient's exam sits squarely in it.
Level by LevelTracing the Territory: Spinal Cord to Pons

The same tracts and nuclei this syndrome touches, followed from where they start in the spinal cord up through the actual lesion level and out the top of the medulla.

Level 1 · Below everything

Sacral Spinal Cord

The starting point. The corticospinal tract (LCST) is already descending toward its synapses, fasciculus gracilis carries lower-extremity proprioception, and the anterolateral system (ALS) has already crossed and is ascending — this far down, that's the whole cast of characters.

Level 2 · Right below the lesion

Cervical Spinal Cord

One level below this patient's lesion, every tract this syndrome touches is already organized: LCST (spared here), the dorsal columns (spared here), ALS (this patient's crossed body loss), and now the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (DSCT) appears — the unconscious-proprioception feed that becomes his ataxia pathway once it reaches the restiform body.

Level 3 · Why the pyramids were spared

Caudal Medulla — Pyramidal Decussation

The corticospinal fibers cross here, at the very caudal tip of the medulla — medial and inferior to where this patient's lesion actually sits. That anatomic separation is exactly why his strength stayed intact: the decussating pyramid is a different structure entirely, nowhere near the dorsolateral territory this syndrome occupies.

Level 4 · Close to the lesion itself

Medulla — Nucleus Ambiguus & ICP

Close to this patient's actual lesion level. Nucleus ambiguus sits in the same lateral territory as the inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) — exactly why one small lesion here can catch both the vagal motor fibers (his hoarseness and palatal droop) and the spinocerebellar afferents (his ataxia) at once.

Level 5 · Moving rostral

Rostral Medulla — CN IX Joins

Glossopharyngeal (CN IX) fibers join the same nucleus ambiguus territory here, right alongside the vestibular nuclei responsible for this patient's vertigo and nystagmus — the densest part of the map for this syndrome's lower-cranial-nerve and vestibular findings.

Level 6 · Where the medulla ends

Pontomedullary Junction

CN VI and VII nuclei appear here for the first time, and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) roots pass through. This patient's facial movement (CN VII) was fully preserved on exam — the key negative finding that keeps the lesion below this junction, confined to the medulla rather than extending into the pons.

BonusOne Level Up — Not This Patient's Pathology
From the same course, a different plate — the caudal pons, one segment rostral to this lesion

Moving one level rostral from the medulla into the caudal pons introduces the abducens (CN VI) and facial (CN VII) nuclei, the pontine corticospinal tract (the same fiber system as the medullary pyramid, renamed at this level), the chief sensory nucleus of CN V (epicritic sensation for the face, a pontine counterpart to the spinal trigeminal tract's pain/temperature role), the trigeminal motor nucleus (motor to the muscles of mastication via V3), and the pontocerebellar tract linking cortex to cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncle. This patient's lesion never reached this level — his facial movement (CN VII) was fully preserved on exam, which is itself one of the negatives that kept the localization anchored in the medulla rather than the pons. Included here for orientation to what's immediately above this case's territory, not because it's part of his findings.
